 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2024:000151 

 [2026] IESC 7 

   

 O'Donnell C.J. 

 Dunne J. 

 O'Malley J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 

   

 BETWEEN/ 

 STUART BROPHY 

 APPLICANT/APPELLANT 

   

 AND 

   

 THE DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS, IRELAND AND THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 RESPONDENTS 

   

   

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Gerard Hogan delivered on the 10th day of February 2026 

 

 Introduction 

 1.       While Article 40.1 is perhaps the single most litigated provision of the Constitution, the courts have at times struggled to give a consistent and yet effective interpretation of the principles of equality which this clause contains. This appeal may be said to provide another almost paradigmatical example of the difficulties which the interpretation of Article 40.1 entails. 

 2.       In the present case the applicant is alleged to have committed an indictable offence (namely, robbery, contrary to s. 14 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001) at a time when he was still a minor for the purposes of the Children Act 2001 ("the 2001 Act"), i.e., less than 18 years: see s. 3(1) of the 2001 Act. Section 75 of the 2001 Act gives a judge of the Children Court (i.e., a specialist judge of the District Court) a jurisdiction to deal summarily with any child charged with any indictable offence, save for those offences which must be tried in the Central Criminal Court (such as murder or rape) or manslaughter. 

 3.       The effect of s. 75 of the 2001 Act is that the key difference between the trial of indictable offences in the case of adults on the one hand and that of children on the other, is that whereas the Director of Public Prosecutions is generally given the power to veto such summary disposal in the case of adults, she has no such power in the case of children. In the case of a charge of robbery, the Director is given the power by s. 53 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001 to veto the summary trial of an adult accused. 

 4.       It is otherwise in the case of children, as s. 75(1) of the 2001 Act provides that the Children Court may deal summarily with an indictable offence unless the Court is of opinion that the offence does not constitute a minor offence fit to be tried summarily. (For convenience and to avoid confusion I propose to describe the Children Court as the District Court in the remainder of this judgment). Where the child does not elect for jury trial, then, in the case of indictable offences coming within s. 75, it is the judge of the Court who must make the decision as to whether the child is to be tried summarily. In this respect the District Court must have regard to factors such as "the age and level of maturity of the child concerned": see s. 75(2)(a). 

 5.       In the present case the applicant was just 17 years of age at the time of the alleged offence which is said to have taken place on 15 th April 2019. The accused is alleged to have acted as a "lookout" in respect of the robbery and it is contended that his co-accused (a much older male) forced a shopworker to open a shop till and some 300 was then stolen. The applicant was originally arrested and detained by a member of An Garda Síochána on 19 th February 2020. This delay was apparently caused by the fact that the investigating Garda had been injured for some of this period. There were also difficulties in making contact with the applicant. 

 6.       The applicant turned 18 years of age in March 2020. In the meantime, the file had been sent to the Garda Youth Diversion Office in August 2020, but as the applicant subsequently failed to meet with his designated Juvenile Liaison Officer, he was deemed unsuitable for inclusion in the Garda Youth Diversion Programme. The file was ultimately returned to the Director of Public Prosecutions. A prosecution was directed on 16 th February 2022 and the matter then came before the District Court in March 2022. As the applicant was by that stage well over 18 years of age, s. 75 of the 2001 Act did not apply. The Director did not consent to summary trial and the applicant was, by a decision of the District Court, then returned to the Circuit Court for arraignment and trial. The applicant then commenced judicial review proceedings in which he challenged the constitutionality of the relevant provisions of s. 75 of the 2001 Act, on Article 40.1 equality grounds insofar as he has been deprived of its benefits by reason of the fact that he is now an aged out minor. 

 7.       Before proceeding further, it should be observed that this is another case of an alleged unconstitutionality by omission. As the applicant would not obtain any practical benefit by the positive invalidation of the relevant provisions of s. 75(1) and s. 75(2), the claim essentially amounts to the contention that by failing to cater for the position of aged out minors, the Oireachtas has thereby breached the equality provisions of Article 40.1. 

 Section 75 of the 2001 Act and the earlier case law 

 8.       Section 75 of the 2001 Act is an enlightened and benevolent provision designed to reflect the immaturity of juvenile offenders. It may be said to represent an endeavour by the Oireachtas to give effect to Article 42A.1 by protecting the rights of children in this way. Unfortunately, however, the Oireachtas when enacting the 2001 Act failed to address one obvious issue, namely, what should happen to the young offender who commits - or is alleged to have committed - a crime as a minor but who is only charged and prosecuted upon reaching adulthood. It is the failure on the part of the Oireachtas to address this question in the context of these - and other - safeguards and protections provided for children by the 2001 Act that has given rise to a series of important recent decisions of this Court: see The People (Director of Public Prosecution) v. CC [2025] IESC 11 ; The People (Director of Public Prosecutions) v. PB [2025] IESC 12 ; Doe (No. 1, 2 and 3) v. Director of Public Prosecutions [2025] IESC 17 .                

 9.       It is important to note, however, that in none of these cases was the constitutionality of these features of the 2001 Act actually at issue, whether by reference to Article 40.1 or otherwise. The absence of any challenge to the constitutionality of the relevant provisions of s. 75 of the 2001 Act meant that these provisions enjoyed the presumption of constitutionality, and these earlier decisions were naturally premised on that basis. In addition, as O'Malley J. notes at paragraph 98 of her judgment, the question of the proper interpretation of s. 75(2) "was not disposed of in Doe ." This, as we shall see, is a critical consideration so far as any evaluation of the constitutional question is concerned. The present case is furthermore quite different from those earlier cases in that unlike the earlier cases the applicant has in fact challenged the constitutionality of these provisions. It is this question which is now directly before this Court. Accordingly, therefore, I consider that the issue of the constitutionality of s. 75 is res integra and must now be considered for the first time by this Court. 

 10.   There has already been one case, however, where a cognate Article 40.1 equality issue arose in relation to the sentencing provisions contained in s. 96(2) and (3) of the 2001 Act and their interaction with the mandatory life sentence provisions in respect of murder contained in s. 2 of the Criminal Justice Act 1990. In Musueni v. Ireland [2024] IEHC 523 , Simons J. held that the then prevailing mandatory life sentence provisions for murder were unconstitutional so far as aged out minors were concerned. This was a case where an "aged out" minor was charged with murder. Had he been tried and convicted while he was still underage, the trial court would have had the option of imposing a lesser sentence than the mandatory life sentence for murder as otherwise prescribed by s. 2 of the Criminal Justice Act 1990 and it could have had regard to his youth and maturity at the time of the murder when imposing such sentence. Conversely, once the accused had attained his majority and was convicted at that point, the trial judge would have had no option but to impose the mandatory life sentence prescribed by the Criminal Justice Act 1990, even though he was a minor at the time of the actual murder. 

 11.   Simons J. held that this differing treatment was contrary to Article 40.1, for - as he explained at para. 55 of his judgment - there was: 

  "[N]o objective justification for the differing treatment afforded to a juvenile offender depending on the happenstance of their age as of the date of sentencing. The point can be illustrated by taking the example of two youths. Suppose that the two youths are the same age and carry out a murder jointly while under the age of eighteen years. Further suppose that, for logistical reasons, separate trials are directed, and that the chronology is such that one youth is sentenced prior to reaching his eighteenth birthday, with the other youth being sentenced as an adult. The effect of the legislation is such that only the first youth would be entitled to rely on his age and level of maturity as a mitigating factor. The second youth would be subject to a mandatory life sentence. The difference of treatment eventuates notwithstanding that the two youths are the same age and were found guilty of the same murder. Crucially, this difference in treatment is logically incapable of supporting the legislative purpose underlying this strand of the sentencing principles, namely that the potential that the moral culpability of a juvenile offender may be less than that of an adult offender should be taken into account in sentencing." 

 12.   In my view, these are the guiding principles so far as the application of Article 40.1 to the present case is concerned. One might add that, as O'Malley J. observed in Donnelly v. Minister for Social Protection [2022] IESC 31 , [2023] 2 IR 415 at 480 (at para. 188), Article 40.1 "provides protection against [legislative] discrimination that is based on arbitrary, capricious or irrational considerations." This decision provides a clear link back to another decision of this Court with some relevance to the present case, namely, Cox v. Ireland [1992] 2 IR 503. In that case it was held that s. 34 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 was unconstitutional in that it provided for the mandatory forfeiture of a public servant's pension entitlements upon conviction in the Special Criminal Court. Had the plaintiff been convicted of the same offence (in that case, a firearms offence) in the ordinary courts, the mandatory disqualification would not apply. In his judgment, Finlay C.J. noted that ([1992] 2 IR 503 at 524) the "ultimate factor triggering the operation of s. 34 in any particular case is the venue of the trial which results in the conviction for a scheduled offence." This was a matter over which the accused had no control. Finlay C.J. held that in those circumstances the section was "impermissibly wide and indiscriminate." 

 The nature and purpose of s. 75 of the 2001 Act 

 13.   It is against this background that we may examine the purpose and effect of s. 75 of the 2001 Act. Section 75 is concerned with the jurisdiction of the District Court to deal with indictable offences on a summary basis. The relevant statutory context has already been helpfully set out by O'Malley J. at paragraphs 98-104 of her judgment. At one level it could be said that, for the reasons which O'Malley J. enunciates, s. 75 is a purely procedural provision which is concerned with the allocation of jurisdiction in respect of the trial of indictable offences. If this were indeed a purely procedural provision then there might, in principle, be few grounds for constitutional objection, even if the Oireachtas was to prescribe different rules in respect of aged out minors by comparison with children. 

 14.   An example here is provided by s. 75(4)(a) of the 2001 Act which provides that in deciding whether or not to consent to summary trial - where the court has decided that this is otherwise appropriate - a child "may obtain the assistance of his or her parent or guardian..." One can well understand that this provision is one which can legitimately be confined to defendants who were still minors at the date they were called upon to make the election in respect of whether they should seek a trial on indictment. There is accordingly no need for this protective provision to apply to the aged out accused, irrespective of when the offence is said to have occurred. 

 15.   This point may be illustrated by the following example. Let us assume that both X and Y are both aged 16 when they are alleged to have participated in the commission of an indictable offence. Now let us assume further that they are subsequently charged at different times so that X was underage at the time he came before the District Court, while Y had attained his majority by the time he was charged. In my view, it is perfectly legitimate for the Oireachtas to say that the s. 75(4)(a) protection (i.e., the right to take parental advice re the right of election as to the mode of trial) should apply in the case of X (the minor accused) only. Why? The answer, I suggest, is that the Oireachtas could legitimately take the view that that protection was no longer necessary where Y in this example had reached the age of eighteen, irrespective of when the offence was alleged to have been committed. It could equally legitimately say that now that Y was aged eighteen he was sufficiently mature to make that decision for himself and that he did not need the assistance of his parents for this purpose. 

 16.    Can this be said of the provisions of s. 75(1) and s. 75(2) which are at the heart of the present challenge? To some degree this depends on the meaning of the words in s. 75(2), namely, "In deciding whether to try or deal with a child summarily for an indictable offence" the Court shall take account of "the age and level of maturity of the child concerned." These words could, as O'Malley J. observes at paragraph 101 of her judgment, be said to be directed to the question of whether it would be appropriate to have the child accused tried in the somewhat more formal - and perhaps even forbidding - atmosphere of the Circuit Court, with all the ceremony that attends a jury trial. There is also the fact that, as O'Malley J. also observed in Doe (No. 1, 2 and 3) v. Director of Public Prosecutions (at para. 130), trial in the Children Court "will be swifter than trial on indictment in the Circuit Court" and these are factors which bear on the potential rehabilitation of any young offender given his immaturity. 

 17.   While these would certainly be relevant considerations for any court called upon to exercise its s. 75(2) jurisdiction, it would, I think, nonetheless be unrealistic to suggest that these are the only considerations which may legitimately inform the court's decision on whether or not to direct summary trial for the purposes of this subsection. There is, to my mind, no doubt but that the question of possible sentence would loom large in any decision of this nature. The reference in s. 75(2) to the age and level of maturity of the child directly echoes the language of the sentencing provisions of s. 96(3) which provides: "A court may take into consideration as mitigating factors a child's age and level of maturity in determining the nature of any penalty imposed, unless the penalty is fixed by law." 

 18.    The child's age and lack of maturity at the time of the commission of the offence renders him less morally culpable than the adult offender. This consideration naturally informs questions of sentencing (s. 96(3)), but it also clearly informs considerations of venue for the purposes of s. 75(2). It is precisely because the offender is a child at the time of the commission of the offence that the sentence is likely to be lower than in the case of a comparable adult offender. This in turn means that the District Court is more likely to deal with the case summarily than with a comparable adult offender. As O'Malley J. observed in Doe (No. 1, 2 and 3) (at para. 130), the effect of a decision in favour of summary trial is that "the child can be immediately assured than no sentence greater than 12 months detention will be imposed." The corollary, of course, is that a higher sentence can be imposed by the Circuit Court if there is a return for trial in that court. 

 19.   There is, of course, no doubt but that should the Circuit Court proceed to conviction in this case, that Court will equally be informed by the relevant s. 96 sentencing principles, so that, irrespective of venue, the fact of the offender's youth and level of maturity at the time of the offence will be a central consideration so far as sentence is concerned, irrespective of the jurisdiction of the trial court. At the same time, however, the prospect of a heavier sentence than might otherwise have been imposed had the case remained in the District Court is a very real one. In the present case, the Director did not consent to summary trial. One can only assume that she took the view that the higher sentencing options which would be available to the Circuit Court following conviction would be (or, at least, might be) appropriate in the present case. 

 20.   If this is the case, then in my view, the principles articulated in both Cox and Musueni apply by analogy in the context of the present claim. The effect of the non-application of s. 75(1) and s. 75(2) to the applicant's case means that he stands exposed to the prospect of higher penalties by reason simply of the date of the prosecution and the general vagaries of the criminal justice system over which he may have no direct control of the result. In the present case, Phelan J found (at para. 80) that had the applicant come before the District Court when he was still a minor that he would, as a matter of probability, have been dealt with by that Court on a summary basis. 

 21.    In the present case the delays were caused, as we have seen, by a variety of factors, some of which seem to have been caused by the applicant, but equally some of them were not: the unavailability of the relevant Garda, coupled with the applicant's (apparently deliberate) unavailability; his refusal to engage with the Juvenile Liaison Officer; and bureaucratic delays in the processing of certain files. One way or another, however, it was the fact that the applicant's case was not processed - for whatever reason - in the District Court before his eighteenth birthday which has brought about the result whereby he faces a higher range of sentence by reason of factors which are, to some degree at least, outside of his control. 

 22.   This, in my view, is the essentially arbitrary feature of the operation of s. 75 of the 2001 Act in respect of which the applicant is entitled to complain. Had the applicant been processed within the criminal justice system while still a juvenile he would more likely have been dealt with summarily and have received a lower sentence. As things stand, the applicant is deprived of the benefits of s. 75 by reason of the fact that he was not dealt with in the District Court while he still remained a juvenile. It is true that, as O'Malley J. has noted in her judgment, the position of the applicant differs in a number of significant, relevant ways by virtue of the fact that he has become an adult in the meantime. Yet, in my respectful opinion, this is not true so far as the issue of sentence is concerned. He is exposed to the prospect of a higher sentence following trial on indictment simply because he is now over 18 years of age and because (for whatever reason) the charge against him was not processed against him while he was still a minor. I think, therefore, that, in the words of Douglas J. in United States v. Peltier (1975) 422 US 531 at 534 (and adopted by Griffin J.  in Murphy v. Attorney General [1982] IR 241 at 327), "[e]qual justice does not permit a defendant's fate to depend upon such a fortuity." While these words were uttered in the somewhat different context of the date upon which a finding of unconstitutionality might take effect, they are nonetheless apposite to the present case where the range of sentencing options may well depend on the vagaries of the criminal justice system and, specifically, the date on which the applicant was processed by that system. 

 23.   It is also important to state that this is not a case of age discrimination as such. In our most recent decision touching on this question, ZG v. Ireland [2025] IESC 49 , all members of the Court were agreed that, in principle, at least the Oireachtas was entitled to differentiate between minors and adults in a range of different areas. The Court divided on the slightly separate question of whether adequate safeguards had been provided for a minor child following the death of his mother in tragic circumstances. On this point the majority judgment of O'Donnell C.J. concluded - applying (at paragraphs 51-52) the rationality test posited by O'Malley J. in Donnelly - that it was rational for the Oireachtas to conclude that the right to succeed to a tenancy in the case of a deceased family member should be confined to adults. 

 24.     As I have just observed, the present case is not an age discrimination as such. It is rather a case where the discrimination occurs by reason of the happenstance of factors related to age. No one doubts that the Oireachtas is entitled to provide for the separate treatment of adult and juvenile offenders. The present case is rather a different one compared to that which obtained in ZG : it is rather that a juvenile offender should not stand exposed to a potentially higher range of sentences simply by reason of the date on which his case happens to be processed within the criminal justice system. 

 Conclusions 

 25.    I consider that s. 75(2) is a provision which is not simply directed to the mode of trial, but is one which also potentially impacts on the question of sentence in a very real way. It is for this - and for this reason alone - that I consider that s. 75(2) operates in the unfair and arbitrary fashion which I have endeavoured to describe. If s. 75(2) was simply a procedural provision concerned with the mode of trial and was one with no implications for sentence, then different considerations would have obtained. 

 26.   It is for that reason that I consider that the applicant is entitled to say that s. 75(2) fails to match up to the standard required by Article 40.1. While I would not grant a declaration which positively invalidates this subsection, I would nevertheless hold that it is unconstitutional by omission in that it fails to address the position of the young offender who is alleged to have committed an indictable offence while still a child, but who is only charged and prosecuted after attaining his majority. 

 27.    It follows, therefore, that I would have to that extent allowed the appeal.
